Title: Spouses' prenatal autonomous motivation to have a child and postpartum depression symptoms.
Source: Journal of clinical psychology (2018)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES: Maternal postpartum depression symptoms (PDS) are linked with negative personal, family, and child developmental outcomes. However, paternal PDS, let alone dyadic process, are understudied. Grounded in the Self-Determination Theory of motivation, this longitudinal study examined whether mothers' and fathers' type of prenatal motivation to have a child predicted depression symptoms 3-6 months after birth. METHOD: The data (N = 90 heterosexual couples) were analyzed using the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model. RESULTS: Dyadic analyses showed that a person's prenatal autonomous motivation to have a child significantly predicted own PDS and partner's PDS. Importantly, these finding were equivalent across genders. CONCLUSIONS: The findings highlight the importance of dyadic prenatal motivational processes as antecedents of PDS.

key_findings.finding: The strongest directly relevant longitudinal dyadic study is PMID 27492636 (2016), involving 711 low-income, racially/ethnically diverse couples recruited after birth. Depression was measured at 1, 6, and 12 months postpartum, and sleep quality at 6 months; the abstract does not name the instruments or provide numeric coefficients/effect sizes. In longitudinal path models adjusted for infant birth weight, breastfeeding, race/ethnicity, poverty, education, and immigration status, depressive symptoms at 1 month predicted poorer sleep at 6 months, and 6-month sleep quality in turn predicted depressive symptoms at both 6 and 12 months in partnered mothers and fathers and single mothers. Thus, sleep predicted persistence/continuation beyond 6 months, but the reciprocal path (early depression → later sleep problems) was also present, supporting a bidirectional/vicious-cycle interpretation rather than sleep-only causation.

The same 711-couple longitudinal path model provides direct evidence relevant to parent-to-parent crossover: maternal and paternal sleep and depressive symptoms were correlated, and maternal sleep quality predicted paternal depressive symptoms at both 6 and 12 months postpartum. This supports prospective maternal-sleep-to-father-depression transmission/crossover, although the retrieved abstract does not report the standardized path coefficients, confidence intervals, or whether paternal baseline depression was included in that specific path.

Other longitudinal couple studies identified in the search support partner depressive-symptom interdependence but do not directly test sleep as the predictor: PMID 25524435 followed 200 Hong Kong couples from pregnancy to 6 months postpartum and found prenatal depression and partner depression associated with higher 6-month depression in both parents; PMID 36973695 reports that partner depressive symptoms can predict early postpartum symptoms, while a longitudinal literature summary suggests paternal prenatal depression predicted worsening maternal depression more consistently than the reverse. These are relevant crossover context but should not be treated as evidence that sleep mediates or causes crossover.

A search result for PMID 34169272 indicates a father-focused study using both subjective and objective sleep measures and links lower perceived sleep quality with postpartum depressive symptoms in fathers, but the retrieved record does not establish longitudinal temporal prediction or provide enough design/effect detail; it should be classified as insufficient for prediction and possibly concurrent association only until full text is reviewed.
